theory.overview: Recursion is a problem-solving technique where a function calls itself to solve smaller instances of the same problem. A recursive solution requires a base case (termination condition) and a recursive case that breaks the problem into smaller subproblems. Recursion naturally handles tree/graph traversals, divide-and-conquer algorithms, and problems with recursive mathematical definitions.

keyConcepts.name: Base Case
keyConcepts.description: The condition that stops recursion. Without it, the function calls itself infinitely causing a stack overflow.

keyConcepts.name: Recursive Case
keyConcepts.description: The function calls itself with a smaller input, moving closer to the base case with each call.

keyConcepts.name: Call Stack
keyConcepts.description: Each recursive call adds a stack frame. Understanding stack depth is crucial for avoiding stack overflow.

keyConcepts.name: Tail Recursion
keyConcepts.description: When the recursive call is the last operation. Some compilers optimize this to use constant stack space.

complexity.time: Varies by problem (often exponential without memoization)

algorithmSteps.description: Call fib(5) - need to compute fib(4) + fib(3)
fib(5) calls fib(4) - not base case, recurse deeper
fib(4) calls fib(3) - continue down left branch
fib(3) calls fib(2) - approaching base cases
fib(3) calls fib(1), base case returns 1
